<thought>We observed a white precipitate when the unknown solution was mixed with AgNO₃, and this precipitate did not dissolve upon addition of NH₃, indicating it is not AgCl. A Ba(NO₃)₂ test gave no precipitate, ruling out sulfate and carbonate (which would form BaSO₄ or BaCO₃). Adding KOH produced a white precipitate, suggesting the cation forms an insoluble white hydroxide (e.g., Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, or Pb²⁺). Among the possible cations, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, and Pb²⁺ give no characteristic flame color, matching the flame‑test result. To distinguish among them, we can add dilute HCl to the KOH precipitate: Al(OH)₃ dissolves only in strong acid, Zn(OH)₂ dissolves readily, and Pb(OH)₂ also dissolves. However, a more definitive test is to add ammonium sulfide ((NH₄)₂S). Zn²⁺ forms a white ZnS precipitate, Pb²⁺ forms a black PbS precipitate, while Al³⁺ does not precipitate. Performing this test will identify the cation. Then, to confirm the anion, we can add dilute HCl to the original AgNO₃ precipitate; if CO₃²⁻ is present, the precipitate will dissolve with effervescence (CO₂ evolution). If the precipitate remains, the anion is likely a non‑reactive one such as NO₃⁻, but NO₃⁻ does not give a precipitate with Ag⁺, so the remaining plausible anion is SO₄²⁻, which we already ruled out. Therefore, after the cation test, the anion can be inferred as the one that gave the AgNO₃ white precipitate—most consistent with carbonate (Ag₂CO₃). Combining the cation (Al³⁺) with the carbonate anion gives aluminum carbonate, Al₂(CO₃)₃, which is a plausible inorganic salt. Hence the identified salt is Al³⁺ with CO₃²⁻. 

Final answer: {"cation": "Al+3", "anion": "CO3-2"}
